title: GPT in Game Theory Experiments
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether GPT-4 can be used as a subject in strategic game experiments and whether its behavior resembles patterns commonly observed in human behavioral economics research. The author focuses on two classic repeated games—the ultimatum game and the prisoner’s dilemma—and asks how prompting GPT with different traits (fairness concern versus selfishness) affects its choices and explanations. The broader question is whether large language models can serve as useful tools for social science experiments and simulations.

The intervention is not an educational one; instead, the study uses the OpenAI Chat Completions API with the gpt-4-1106-preview model to run simulated multi-round games. GPT agents were prompted with role instructions, game rules, prior-round history, and trait framing ("fair" or "selfish"), and were required to generate both a decision and a reasoning statement each round. The author ran 700 total simulated games across treatment combinations in repeated ultimatum and prisoner’s dilemma settings, then analyzed both the game choices and the generated reasoning texts.

There were no human student, teacher, or school participants. The “population” consisted of GPT-4 agents acting as simulated game players in an online/API-based experimental environment. The paper is situated in economics/social science methodology rather than education, writing instruction, formative feedback, or student draft revision. It therefore does not match the requested topic of comparative studies on LLM-generated formative feedback for grades 9–12 student writing.

The main conclusion is that GPT-4 often produces behavior that resembles human-like strategic patterns: positive offers and rejection of unfair offers in the ultimatum game, and condition-dependent cooperation in the prisoner’s dilemma. Prompted traits meaningfully influenced outcomes, with “fair” GPT behaving more cooperatively or generously than “selfish” GPT. The author argues that LLMs may be useful as supplementary tools for experimental social science and social simulation, while also noting limitations such as prompt sensitivity and judgment errors in strategic reasoning.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not an education study and does not examine any K-12 instructional intervention, student writing task, or formative feedback process. It is an arXiv preprint on GPT behavior in economic game simulations, so it is ineligible for the requested evidence base and does not meet relevance criteria for the K-12 framework.
impact_tier_rationale: No education outcomes are studied, and there is no evidence on grades 9-12 student writing, revision, or feedback effects. Therefore the paper provides no usable impact evidence for the target intervention class.
